The three primitives form a hierarchical diagnostic triad: Resolution quantifies how well forecasts distinguish future outcomes, Two-Group Separation provides a fast rank-order proxy for that discrimination, and Selective-Publish Conditional Brier evaluates performance on strategically defined subsets. Murphy's decomposition isolates these components from total Brier score, enabling rigorous fault-localization. In GSE, Resolution acts as a bottleneck because it measures the model's ability to generate diverse state transitions; in GSI, it maps to posterior variance reduction. The primitives' failure modes—flatness, insufficient separation, and overfitting—are interdependent: improving one often degrades another. Cross-layer veto conditions enforce that improvements in calibration (REL) do not come at the expense of genuine resolution, preventing 'over-certainty' traps where models become perfectly calibrated but useless.
